1163.title: Nanak's twelve months
1163.hook: Guru Nanak's own twelve months, older and more stark than Guru Arjan's (Tukhari, ang 1107)
1163.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in kirtan in Raga Tukhari and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Babarvani closed: faith that sees, looking at a burning town and still calling God the Master. Today the same poet turns to the turning year.

What month is it? The quick answer comes off a phone: a name, a number, a box on a grid. But the Punjab has an older way of naming time, months called Chet and Vaisakh, Savan and Poh, each with its own weather. Guru Nanak wrote a poem through that calendar, a Barah Maha: twelve months of a soul missing its Beloved. You met it once on this path, in a single glance. Over the next few days, it goes season by season. Today, before a single flower opens: how it begins.
screen: `WHAT MONTH IS IT?` → `A CALENDAR WITH WEATHER.` → `NANAK'S TWELVE MONTHS.`

segments.voice: The poem sits in Raga Tukhari, on ang eleven hundred seven of the Guru Granth Sahib, under Guru Nanak's name. First, the frame. It doesn't start with spring. It starts with a word to the listener. In plain English, not word for word: hear this. Each one lives out the deeds done before. On every head comes joy or sorrow, and whatever You give is good. Then the bride speaks. This world is Yours, Lord, so what is my state? Without You I can't live even a moment. Before any month is named, you know who's speaking and what she lacks, and every season is seen through that lack. Second, the sound. Each month gets its own long, unhurried stanza, piling up blossoms, bees, a blazing sun, lightning, frost, then turning again to the same ache: the Beloved is not home. Third, the voice. The Granth holds another Barah Maha, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh, which this path read in year two. Both are true to the same longing. Some readers find Nanak's the starker of the two: heavier weather, a rawer cry, comfort held back until late. Put simply, it's a year where little changes outside while everything inside waits. Spring, the heat, the rains, the cold: each gets its turn. That's today's line: Nanak's months.
screen: `IT OPENS WITH: LISTEN.` · `WHATEVER YOU GIVE IS GOOD.` · `EACH MONTH, THE SAME ACHE.` · `A STARKER VOICE, SOME SAY.` · then, large: `NANAK'S MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Say the name of the month you're in, quietly, the Punjabi one if you know it, or the one you use. Let your breath slow and notice what this month has brought: the light at the window, the air on your skin, what's growing or falling outside. Then name, gently, what you're waiting for this month, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.
Nanak's twelve months. Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in Raga Tukhari, which opens by asking us to listen, then walks the year through a bride's longing. Today's word.
Your line: nanak's months. A whole year of weather, read as one long love. Until tomorrow.

1164.title: Spring's longing
1164.hook: in the spring months the bride hears the koel and longs for the Beloved (Tukhari Barah Maha)
1164.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in each month as the soul's longing for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanak's twelve months: a poem that opens with listen, and a bride who can't live a moment without her Beloved. Today the year begins.

A bird calls from a mango tree, early, before the house is awake. Then again, a little farther off. The poem names it: the koel, singing in the mango tree. Guru Nanak puts it right at the start of his year. The month is Chet, spring, and everything is beautiful. That's the trouble. When the whole world is in bloom, the one thing missing is easier to hear.
screen: `A BIRD IN THE MANGO TREE.` → `CHET: EVERYTHING IN BLOOM.` → `THE MISSING ONE IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Here's Chet, in plain English, not word for word. Chet is good, spring is lovely, the bumblebees are beautiful, the forest is in flower. Then the koel sings sweetly in the mango tree, and the bride asks: how can I bear this pain inside me? The bumblebee circles the flowering branch, and she says, how can I live, mother? I'm dying. Notice: the poem doesn't call spring bad. It calls it lovely. But when the one you love is far away, beauty can hurt more than gray skies. Every lovely thing points at who isn't there to see it. Then Vaisakh, and the trees join in: Vaisakh is good, and the branches put on new clothes, fresh leaves like an outfit for a wedding. And the bride stands looking at the door. Come home, Beloved, have mercy. Carry me across this hard ocean. Without You, I'm not worth half a shell. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul and the Beloved is God. So spring is the moment life is fullest around you, and something in you still says: not yet, not without You. The poem doesn't shush that. It treats the ache as part of love, the sign she hasn't forgotten who she's waiting for. That's today's line: the bird calls.
screen: `CHET: THE KOEL IN THE MANGO TREE.` · `BEAUTY CAN MAKE MISSING LOUDER.` · `VAISAKH: BRANCHES IN NEW CLOTHES.` · `THE BRIDE WATCHES THE DOOR.` · then, large: `THE BIRD CALLS.`

segments.voice: Open a window or step outside if you can, or just listen to the room, and wait for a bird, any bird, near or far. If one calls, follow the sound until it fades; if none comes, notice the waiting itself, the leaning-in, the small hope, the bride at the door. If you pray, say Waheguru softly between the calls.
Spring's longing. In Guru Nanak's Chet and Vaisakh, the koel sings and the trees put on new clothes, and all that beauty makes the absent Beloved felt more. Today's word.
Your line: the bird calls. Spring is lovely, and still the bride watches the door. That's today, done.

1165.title: Summer's heat
1165.hook: the hot months burn the one who is apart (Tukhari Barah Maha)
1165.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it in the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in the hot months as the soul's thirst for God's nearness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spring's longing: the koel in the mango tree, and beauty that made the missing one louder. Today the blossoms are gone, and the sun takes over.

Noon, and the road shimmers. A dog lies flat in the one strip of shade by the wall. Nobody walks if they don't have to. Guru Nanak's year walks straight into that heat. Two months, Jeth and Asarh, and in both the earth is burning. Yet read closely, and the poem calls the months good. So what, exactly, is burning?
screen: `NOON, AND THE ROAD SHIMMERS.` → `JETH AND ASARH.` → `SO WHAT IS BURNING?`

segments.voice: Jeth first, in plain English, not word for word. The month of Jeth is good. How could the Beloved be forgotten? The lands are hot as a furnace, and the bride offers her prayer. Then Asarh, heavier still. The sun blazes in the sky. The earth suffers and dries out, roasted by fire. The sun doesn't give up its work; its chariot keeps circling. The bride looks for shade. Out in the wild, a cricket calls. Three things to notice. First, the months are still called good. Nanak isn't complaining about summer; heat is the month doing what it does, like the sun at its work. Second, the heat pictures something inside. The earth is parched, and so is the bride. Being apart from the one you love has its own dryness, a thirst a glass of water can't touch. Third, look at what she does. In Jeth she prays. In Asarh she looks for shade. She doesn't pretend she's fine, and she doesn't give up; she moves toward the one cool place there is. In Sikh reading, that shade is the Beloved's nearness, the remembrance of God's Name. And the stanza keeps one small detail for the end: a cricket calling in the heat. The bride hears it. She's calling too. That's today's line: the heat of apart.
screen: `JETH: THE LANDS BURN LIKE A FURNACE.` · `STILL, THE MONTH IS CALLED GOOD.` · `THE INNER HEAT OF BEING APART.` · `THE BRIDE LOOKS FOR SHADE.` · then, large: `THE HEAT OF APART.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or run a little cool water over your wrists, and feel the coolness as your breath slows. As it fades, notice any dry or heated place in you today, a worry, a distance from someone, a thirst you can name, and let the cool and the thirst sit side by side without fixing anything. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath, like stepping into shade.
Summer's heat. In Guru Nanak's Jeth and Asarh, the earth burns, the months are still called good, and the bride, parched by being apart, looks for shade. Today's word.
Your line: the heat of apart. Even in the burning months, there is shade. See you tomorrow.

1166.title: The rains
1166.hook: the rain falls, and the bride waits (Tukhari Barah Maha)
1166.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it in the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's sleepless rainy nights as the soul's waiting for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heat of apart: Jeth and Asarh, the earth burning, and the bride looking for shade. Today the heat breaks, and the sky opens.

The first drops hit the dust and you can smell it before you see it. Then the whole sky lets go. After the burning months, the rains should be pure relief, and Guru Nanak's poem starts out that way. In the month of Savan it says, in plain English: be glad, my mind, the clouds are pouring, the season has come. Then, in the very same stanza, the gladness cracks.
screen: `THE FIRST DROPS ON THE DUST.` → `SAVAN: BE GLAD, MY MIND.` → `THEN THE GLADNESS CRACKS.`

segments.voice: Here's how Savan goes on, not word for word. I love my Lord with body and mind, but my Love has gone to a far country. He doesn't come home, and I'm dying of sighs. The lightning flashes, and it frightens me. My bed is empty, and it hurts. The rain that cools the earth doesn't reach her. What everyone longed for has arrived; the one she longs for hasn't. Then Bhadon, the second rainy month, darker and louder. Rain falls in the black of night. Land and water brim. Frogs and peacocks cry out. A bird called the papiha calls, beloved, beloved. Snakes slither about, biting; mosquitoes sting. A night full of noise, and none of it the voice she's waiting for. Notice the papiha: its call is the bride's own word. The bird does out loud what she does inside. And notice the honesty. The rain is beautiful and frightening at once, the lightning and the snakes right beside the brimming pools. Waiting here isn't calm. It's lying awake while the storm goes on. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul and the Beloved is God. Even a season of plenty can be a season of waiting, and waiting doesn't mean she has stopped loving. That's today's line: waiting in rain.
screen: `SAVAN: MY LOVE IS IN A FAR COUNTRY.` · `THE LIGHTNING FRIGHTENS HER.` · `BHADON: A LOUD, DARK NIGHT.` · `THE PAPIHA CALLS: BELOVED.` · then, large: `WAITING IN RAIN.`

segments.voice: Watch the rain if it's falling, or close your eyes and bring it to mind: the first drops on dust, the smell, the steady sound on a roof. Let your breath settle into that sound, and let one thing you're still waiting for sit in the rain with you; you don't have to feel calm about it. If you pray, say Waheguru with each breath, like the papiha's call.
The rains. Guru Nanak's Savan and Bhadon, where the clouds pour and the land brims, and the bride lies awake, waiting for the one who hasn't come home. Today's word.
Your line: waiting in rain. Tomorrow, the year turns cold. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1167.title: Winter's union
1167.hook: in the cold months the Beloved comes home (Tukhari Barah Maha)
1167.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it in the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's meeting in the cold months as the soul finding God within by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, waiting in rain: Savan and Bhadon, lightning and a papiha calling beloved, and a bride still loving through the storm.

A key turns in the door late on a winter night. Coats come off, someone puts the kettle on, and the cold stays outside where it belongs. Every season so far in Guru Nanak's year has ended in the same place: the bride at the door, and nobody coming. Spring, the bird calls. Summer, she looks for shade. The rains, she lies awake. Winter could have been the loneliest of all. It isn't. Somewhere in the cold months, the key turns.
screen: `A KEY IN THE DOOR.` → `EVERY SEASON, NOBODY CAME.` → `THEN, IN THE COLD, HE DOES.`

segments.voice: Watch the winter stanzas change, in plain English, not word for word. Maghar first: the month is good for the one absorbed in the Lord's virtues. Already the voice is calmer. Then Poh, which this path met earlier: frost falls, and the sap dries in the forest and the grass. The cold is real. Then Magh, and a sentence that turns the whole poem. In Magh I became pure, she says. I came to know the place of pilgrimage is within me. For months she has looked outward, at the door, the road, the sky. Now she stops looking for a holy river far away and finds the sacred place inside. Then Phalgun, the last month, and joy. Her mind delights, love comes easily, joy fills the days and nights, because she has let go of herself. And then: when it pleased Him, in mercy, He came home. Notice the order. She didn't earn the arrival by trying harder. She let go of self, found the holy place within, and the Beloved came as a gift. Notice the weather, too. The poem never says it got warmer first; the frost of Poh is only a few stanzas back. The meeting never depended on the season. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul, the Beloved is God, and home is the heart. That's today's line: he comes home.
screen: `MAGHAR: THE VOICE GROWS CALM.` · `MAGH: THE HOLY PLACE IS WITHIN.` · `PHALGUN: SHE LETS GO OF SELF.` · `IN MERCY, HE CAME HOME.` · then, large: `HE COMES HOME.`

segments.voice: Pull a blanket or a sweater around your shoulders and feel the warmth gather as your breath slows. Then, like the bride in Magh, stop looking outward and notice the quiet place inside, behind the breath, resting there the way you'd rest once you're home and the door is shut. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.

1168.title: Twelve months close
1168.hook: two poets, twelve months each, one longing
1168.howItsDone: Both Barah Mahas are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; in some gurdwaras Guru Arjan's stanza for the new month is read on Sangrand, the first day of the month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he comes home: in the cold months the bride found the holy place within, let go of self, and in mercy the Beloved came.

Two and ten. That's how the last stanza of Guru Nanak's poem counts the months: not twelve, but be das, two and ten, the way someone might count on their fingers at the end of a long year. Once the Beloved has come home, the poem looks back over all of it. And the Guru Granth Sahib holds a second year like it, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh. Two poets, twelve months each.
screen: `TWO AND TEN.` → `NANAK LOOKS BACK OVER THE YEAR.` → `A SECOND YEAR, BY GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of Nanak's year, not word for word. The two and ten months, the seasons, the dates, the days are good. The hours, the moments, the instants are blessed, when the True One comes and the meeting happens with ease. Hold that beside the whole year. Spring was good, and she ached. The hot months were good, and she burned. The rains were good, and she lay awake. Nothing about the weather was wrong. What changed was the meeting, and once it came, every month looked different looking back, even the hard ones. Now set Guru Arjan's year beside it, which this path read in year two. His months are in Raga Majh, and they too move from Chet around to Phalgun, a bride separated and asking to be united. In his Chet, remembering the Lord brings joy. In his Asarh, the heat burns the ones who don't keep the Lord near. Two Gurus, two ragas, two voices, sharing the same bones: a calendar the farmer and the bride both know, a longing in every month, and an ending where time itself is blessed. That's what a Barah Maha does. It doesn't wait for one perfect season. It takes the ordinary year, every page of it, and lets each month carry the same love. Not one season is left out. That's today's line: every season longs.

1169.title: The ballad in Majh
1169.hook: Guru Nanak's Var in Majh with saloks (ang 137–150)
1169.tomorrow: The dark age is a knife
1169.howItsDone: Majh ki Var is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib; in a var, the saloks and pauris are sung or read together, the salok first and then the pauri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every season longs: Nanak's year closed with every month blessed, and Guru Arjan's year shared its bones. This week the Babarvani ended, and the koel's spring turned into the Beloved coming home.

A singer at a village fair, a drum, and a story of two fighters, sung verse after verse while the crowd leans in. Tradition says that's what a var was in the Punjab: a ballad of heroes and battles, sung loud. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Majh, and there's a var by Guru Nanak, with a heading naming the tune it's sung to, after two figures from a ballad. Same drum, same shape. But the battle inside is a different kind.
screen: `A SINGER, A DRUM, TWO FIGHTERS.` → `A VAR: A BALLAD.` → `GURU NANAK'S VAR IN MAJH.`

segments.voice: Start with the shape. A var in the Granth is built from pauris, stanzas, and some readers hear in pauri the word for a step, as on a ladder; each pauri moves the ballad up one rung. Between them sit saloks, short verses that set up or answer each step. In Majh ki Var, some saloks carry Guru Nanak's name and some Guru Angad's, so two Gurus' voices meet in one ballad. Next, the tune. The heading says to sing it to the tune of Malik Murid and Chandrahara Sohia. Tradition remembers them as heroes of a folk ballad, a song people already knew. So the Guru took a sound the crowd could hum and filled it with something new. Then the opening. Before any battle, the first salok is about the Guru. In plain English, not word for word: the Guru is the giver. The Guru is a house of ice, a cool place in the heat. The Guru is the lamp of the three worlds, a gift that never runs out, and the one whose mind trusts the Guru finds peace. Giver, coolness, lamp: after a week of burning summers and dark rainy nights, this ballad opens with shade and light. And where a war song might open by praising a hero, this one praises the Guru, the one who shows the way. The fights that follow are inner ones: with ego, with falsehood, with a broken age. That's today's line: the majh ballad.
screen: `PAURIS: STEPS, LIKE A LADDER.` · `SUNG TO A FOLK BALLAD'S TUNE.` · `THE GURU: GIVER, ICE, LAMP.` · `THE BATTLE INSIDE.` · then, large: `THE MAJH BALLAD.`

segments.voice: If you can, play the opening of Majh ki Var, sung or recited; if not, sit with its three pictures. Breathe in: giver; breathe out: a cool house of ice; breathe in: a lamp, letting each one rest a few breaths. Notice which one you need most today, and if you pray, say Waheguru beside it.
The ballad in Majh. Guru Nanak's var, a ballad in steps called pauris, with saloks between them, sung to an old ballad's tune and opening with the Guru as giver, coolness and lamp. Today's word.
Your line: the majh ballad. A ballad's drum, and a battle fought inside. See you tomorrow.
